full_judgment:
7. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff on the other hand, submitted that by and under the provisions of Admiralty Court Act, 1861 passed by the Parliament in England, the High Court of Admiralty would have all Jurisdiction over any claim for damages done by any ship and High Court of Admiralty in England having exercised its jurisdiction ever since, for the last few centuries, over matters within Internal Waters as well as on High Seas, the same would be exercised by the Colonial Admiralty Court and therefore by the present Admiralty Court of Bangladesh having succeeded to all those powers exercised by the High Court of Admiralty in England, and also by the Colonial Court of Admiralty. In support of this contention Mr. Asrarul Hossain referred to a number of decisions to which I shall advert at the relevant portion of the Judgment. Mr. Hossain has further submitted that the provisions of Inland Shipping Ordinance, 1976 referred to by the defendants has been promulgated not to supersede the age-old jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court in matters between the vessel and the ships within its territorial jurisdiction in relation to a cause of action which arose in whatever waters it might be, but rather the scheme of the Inland Shipping Ordinance had been of a supervisory character and aims at the control of navigation of vessels plying in Inland Waters and for its proper registration having proper documents, providing penalty for loss of life on board the vessel caused by any criminal activity, provide measures for avoiding overloading. These are the limited purposes for which the Ordinance would be applicable and in matters like that in Inland Waters, the parties would go before the Marine Court for adjudication. Marine Court had not been given any jurisdiction to try civil cases or matters arising on tort or cases falling within the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court and the said Ordinance never, impliedly even, admitted to have taken away the rights or the powers under any other provision of law, by narrating that the provisions of the Inland Shipping Ordinance, 1976 would be applicable notwithstanding any other law for the time being in force. The Marine Court is a Criminal Court and looks at the Criminal side of the matter and for further loss there cannot be any issue of any compensation before the Marine Court but only an issue for rash and negligent navigation. 

 8. This submission of the learned Counsel has substance. Admiralty Jurisdiction of this Court to hear and determine Mercantile and marine matters have travelled a long way from the days of the East India Company which sought to decide these sorts of disputes by establishing a Court of Admiralty at Surat. Thereafter in exercise of the power under the Regulating Act, 1773 the King of England vide Letters Patent of 1774 established the Supreme Court at Fort William at Calcutta. The authority of Supreme Court at Fort William was also extended to the high seas and the Court was given the full power to hear and determine all cases of piracy and all Marine cases, caused whatsoever, according to the laws and customs of the Admiralty of England. In 1861 the Admiralty Courts Act was passed in British Parliament providing extended jurisdiction to the High Court of Admiralty in England. In the same year in 1861 by a Letters Patent the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal was established. It abolished the Presidency Supreme Courts and other company Courts such as Sadar Dewani and Nizamat Adalats. The High Court so established under that charter is to exercise all original and appealable powers of civil, criminal, admiralty and all testamentary interests jurisdiction and shall ordinarily apply all such powers and authorities for and in relation to the administration of justice in the Presidency in which it is established as was exercised by the Supreme Court at Fort Williams. In 1891 the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act was enacted by which the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal was declared to be also the Colonial Court of Admiralty. The Admiralty Jurisdiction conferred upon the Colonial Court were precisely the powers that were exercised by the High Court of Admiralty in England. All the said powers were, thus, exercised by the High Court at Calcutta as the Colonial Admiralty Court for long. 

 10. It is thus seen that for the exercise of this Admiralty jurisdiction by this Court, no particular law was enacted either by the present Parliament or by the Parliament of the then Pakistan or even by that of India and in fact the present admiralty power relates back to, and is the cumulative effect of the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act of 1861 and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1891. The provisions of the Admiralty Courts Act of 1861 (24, Victoria, 1861) thereafter, need be referred to, out of necessity, to appreciate the objection as to jurisdiction as argued at the Bar. 

 11. Section 4 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 so also section 5 and 6 of the said Act speaks of the jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty in England over any claim for necessaries supplied to any ship elsewhere than in the Port to which the ship belongs and have jurisdiction over any claim by the owner or consignee or assignee of any bill of lading of any goods carried into any Port in England or Wales in any ship, for damage done to the goods or any part thereof by the negligence or misconduct of, or for any breach of contract on the part of, the owner, master, or crew of the ship, unless it is shown to the satisfaction of the Court that at the time of the institution of the cause any owner of part owner of the ship is domiciled in England or Wales. Section 7 provided that the High Court of Admiralty shall have jurisdiction over any claim for damage done by any ship. Section 12 provided that the High Court of Admiralty shall have the same powers over any British ship or any share therein, as are conferred upon the High Court Chancery in England. Section 13 provided that whenever any ship or vessel or the proceeds thereof are under arrest of the High Court of Admiralty, the said Court shall have the same powers as are conferred upon the High Court of Chancery in England by the Ninth part of The Merchant Shipping Act, 1854. It has been further provided by section 14 that the High Court of Admiralty shall be a Court of Record for all intents and purposes. It has further provided in section 17 that the Judge of the High Court of Admiralty shall have all such powers as are possessed by any of the superior Courts of Common Law or any Judge thereof to compel either party in any cause or matter to answer interrogatories, and to enforce the production, inspection, and delivery of copies of any document in his possession or power. It has been finally provided in section 35 that the jurisdiction conferred by this Act on the High Court of Admiralty may be exercised either by proceedings in rem or by proceedings in personam. 

 "The Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court of Justice, which may be exercised in proceedings in rem or in personam, is co-extensive, geographically, with that of the late High Court of Admiralty from the coming into force of the Admiralty Court Act, 1840, until the jurisdiction of the latter Court was, by the Judicature Act, 1873, Sec. 16, transferred to the High Court of Justice; the geographical extent of the Jurisdiction is world wide The jurisdiction of the Court of Admiralty originally extended to every sort of collision and damage to property occurring upon the high seas and upon tidal waters not within the body of a country. By the Admiralty Court Act, 1840, Sec. 6, its jurisdiction was extended to (amongst other things) claim for damage received by "any ship or sea-going vessel" within the body of a country; and by the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, sec. 2, 7, it was further extended to claims for damage done by "any description of vessel used in navigation not propelled by oars". It appears that these statutes covered every case of collision between craft of all sorts, except a collision within the body of a country between lighters or other craft both of which were propelled by oars only". 

 14. It is, thus, clear from the passage as above that by the Admiralty Court Act, 1840 the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court was extended to all claims for damage received by any ship or sea-going vessel within the body of a country and subsequently the expression "ship" had been clearly defined in section 7 of the Admiralty Act, 1861 to include any description of vessel used in navigation not propelled by oars. Therefore, the provision covers all cases of collision between craft of all sorts within the body of a country or outside except a collision between lighters or other craft both of which were propelled by oars only. 

 15. The case of M.L. Madina Vs. M.L. Jalmani, reported in 30 DLR 149 was a case for damages for irresponsible plying of vessel causing damage to the plaintiff within the internal waters at river Meghna. In that case the defendant challenges the jurisdiction of this Court to attend to the Admiralty Suit on the ground that it does not extend to Inland Waters of the river, the Meghna. Abdullah, J. in rejecting this preliminary objection raised in that Admiralty Suit No. 1 of 1966 vide judgment and order dated 15th August, 1966, which judgment and order had not been reported, held in the relevant portion thus: 

 "There was no definition of ship or seagoing vessel in the said Act. The said Act was however, modified by the Admiralty Act of 1861, 24 and 25 Victoris C 10. This Act was enacted to extend the jurisdiction and improve the practice of the High Court of Admiralty. 

 Section 2 of the 1861 Act defines "ship" as follows: 

 Section 7 lays down that the High Court of Admiralty shall have jurisdiction over any claim for damage done by any ship. The original jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty as conferred by section 6 of the 1840 Act was therefore extended to non-sea going vessels also. The High Court of Admiralty had, already as a Court of Admiralty, according to the previous Act, jurisdiction over causes of action, arising in inland waters but in the 1840 Act it was confined only to ship or sea-going vessels from which it might have been inferred that the jurisdiction was confined to causes of action relating to sea-going vessels. That doubt has been set at rest by definition of ship in the 1861 Act." The Court finally decided to hold that the Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
